questions.prompt: Why is the FileAccessed versus FileDownloaded distinction forensically important?
options: They are synonyms in cloud audit logs
They mean genuinely different things -- tooling reading a file via API can generate the former without the latter, so reporting access as exfiltration overstates the incident
FileAccessed is always malicious and FileDownloaded never is
Only FileDownloaded is logged by default
questions.explanation: Conflating the two either inflates notification scope or misses real transfers. Each is a different claim with different evidentiary weight.

questions.prompt: Why must proxy and NetFlow logs be collected in the first hour?
options: They are deleted the moment an incident is declared
They are frequently retained for days rather than months, and are often the only source able to size an outbound transfer
They can only be read while the incident is active
They require attacker cooperation to obtain
questions.explanation: Short retention means these logs may not exist by the time scoping identifies exactly what to ask for -- so collection precedes full scoping.

questions.prompt: What are the three tiers of the scope statement this playbook produces?
options: Confirmed exfiltrated; accessed but exfiltration not demonstrated; reachable but no access evidence
questions.explanation: Keeping these tiers distinct is the core deliverable. Collapsing them upward inflates cost and notification scope; collapsing them downward is indefensible if evidence later contradicts it.

questions.prompt: Why is encrypted egress traffic still analyzable for exfiltration purposes?
options: Encryption can always be broken during incident response
Volume and destination analysis still work -- you may not see contents, but you can see that a large transfer occurred and where it went
Encrypted traffic is never used for exfiltration
Proxy logs automatically decrypt all traffic
questions.explanation: Content visibility is not required to establish that a substantial transfer occurred to a given destination at a given time, which is often enough to size the incident.
